posts.author: The Decoder
posts.text: Anthropic brings Claude to civilian agencies as its fight with the Pentagon drags on. Anthropic is now offering Claude for Government to US federal and state agencies. The platform runs in a FedRAMP High environment, the strictest US security level for cloud services. Agencies get the same features as enterprise customers, pay for what they use with fixed spending caps, and can set budgets for each department. The Pentagon won't be using it because it still classifies Anthropic as a supply chain risk. posts.author: Bloomberg Tech
posts.text: Markets Face Rising Yields, AI Risks. Get a jump start on the US trading day with Dani Burger on "Bloomberg Open Interest." A new quarter begins with stocks battling a relentless rise in yields. Micron fuels the AI trade, Google rolls out Gemini 4 Argon, and Netflix plots its next act. Plus, Citi’s Kate Moore on why she's betting on stocks, Carlyle’s Mark Jenkins joins us to talk about hidden AI credit risks, and Aston Martin CEO Adrian Hallmark unveils the company's newest luxury SUV as it embarks on the road to a turnaround. (Source: Bloomberg)

posts.author: Bloomberg Tech
posts.text: Suno CEO: AI Could Reinvent How We Experience Music. Suno CEO and Co-Founder Mikey Shulman says AI could transform music from a largely passive experience into one where listeners actively create, remix and collaborate with their favorite artists. With more than 100 million users and partnerships across the music industry, Shulman discusses Suno’s in-house AI models, opportunities around licensing artists’ voices and music, and why he believes AI can expand the music business. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

posts.author: Bloomberg Tech
posts.text: Bloomberg Tech Screentime Special. Bloomberg’s Ed Ludlow is live in LA for Bloomberg Screentime 2026, speaking with tech leaders and media entrepreneurs. Suno CEO Mikey Shulman discusses how AI is expanding — rather than simply disrupting — the music industry, Promise CEO George Strompolos and Luma AI COO Caroline Ingeborn talk about AI's growing role in filmmaking, and Vermillio CEO Dan Neely dives into the debate around AI and creators' rights. (Source: Bloomberg)

posts.author: Bloomberg Tech
posts.text: Promise CEO: AI Lets Smaller Teams Make Bigger Films. Promise CEO and Co-Founder George Strompolos is building what he calls an AI-native entertainment studio, using generative AI across development, production and visual effects. He says the technology can cut costs by more than 50% on some animated projects and allow smaller teams to create productions with far greater scale. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

posts.author: Bloomberg Tech
posts.text: Luma AI Bets on ‘Hybrid’ Future for Hollywood. Luma AI COO Caroline Ingeborn says generative AI could help bring more film and television production back to Los Angeles by lowering costs and giving creators new ways to execute ambitious projects. She discusses why she sees AI as a tool for creative professionals rather than a replacement for them and how “hybrid filmmaking” can combine real actors and crews with AI-generated environments. She joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

posts.author: Bloomberg Tech
posts.text: How Vermillio Tackles AI's Creator Rights Challenge. As AI reshapes the entertainment industry, who controls and gets paid for the use of a creator's work and likeness? Vermillio is tackling that question with technology designed to track and license AI-generated content. Vermillio Co-Founder and CEO Dan Neely joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

posts.author: The Decoder
posts.text: Nearly half of test subjects mistook Tavus' AI video avatar for a real person on a one-minute call. Tavus has introduced Griffin, what the company calls the first "Human Interaction Model." The AI holds video calls in real time, processing facial expressions, tone of voice, and gestures. In a Tavus study, 48 percent of participants believed Griffin was a real person after a one-minute call. Previous systems maxed out at two percent. posts.author: testingcatalog
posts.text: Tavus has introduced Griffin, a research preview of its newest video-to-video model for real-time face-to-face conversations. Griffin is designed to learn conversational behavior from people. Tavus says Griffin is the first model to pass the Turing test, with 45% of 120 study participants taking its conversation as real. On NVIDIA's Video Full-Duplex Benchmark, Griffin Lite ranks first among every model evaluated, at 3.83 out of 5 against 3.92 for real humans.

posts.text: AI agents inadvertently leak 13,000+ internal screenshots from organizations. AI agents have been quietly uploading internal screenshots from over 300 companies to public GitHub repos, some of which contain sensitive information.

posts.author: The Decoder
posts.text: Security startup finds more than 13,000 internal company screenshots that AI agents uploaded publicly. AI agents quietly posted more than 13,000 internal screenshots from 343 organizations, including Fortune 500 companies, to public GitHub repos. Because the platform didn't offer a protected way to upload them, the agents came up with a workaround on their own. The exposed images showed customer data, login credentials, and details about unreleased products. posts.author: Simon Willison
posts.text: He Built This City. I visited the Museum of the City of New York today and got to see He Built This City: Joe Macken’s Model , the 50 x27 feet model of the city built over a 21 year period from balsa wood and cardboard. It exceeded my already high expectations. The exhibition closes on 12th October so you should absolutely make a priority to see it if you get the chance. Tags: museums , new-york
